title: Advanced Analytics
tagline: Metrics, dimensions, grain, conditional aggregation, and cross-tabs — analytics beyond GROUP BY

placementQuiz.q: A report is unique per (date, country). Which word names that row-level uniqueness?
placementQuiz.explain: Grain is the unit of observation a result set is unique by; (date, country) is the grain.

placementQuiz.q: Which aggregate counts distinct buyers, ignoring the rest?
placementQuiz.explain: COUNT(DISTINCT col) counts unique non-null values of col — distinct buyers, not rows.

placementQuiz.q: You need SUM(amount) for paid orders only. If the dialect supports it, the cleanest form is…
options: SUM(CASE WHEN status='paid' THEN amount END)
placementQuiz.explain: FILTER (WHERE …) scopes an aggregate to matching rows and is available in PostgreSQL and modern SQL.

placementQuiz.q: Which statement about a cross-tab pivot is true?
options: It needs a GROUP BY with one row group per horizontal band
It is the same as a self-join
PIVOT is available on all DBs identically
It converts row-dimension values into columns
placementQuiz.explain: A pivot rotates values of a row dimension into separate columns; PostgreSQL uses CASE aggregation or crosstab().

placementQuiz.q: Compute share of total as a percentage. Which expression gives each row's percent of the whole table?
options: amount / (SELECT SUM(amount)) is the only way
placementQuiz.explain: amount / SUM(amount) OVER () divides each amount by the grand-total window sum.

blocks.md: Analytics SQL is the practice of turning transactional events into decision tables. Pick your identifier (user, order, session), pick your metric, be explicit about grain — everything else follows.

A **metric** is a quantifiable number you aggregate (revenue, buyers). A **dimension** is the label you slice by (day, country). The **grain** is the unit of observation a result row is unique by — here, one row per (day, country). Deciding the grain before writing SQL is the decision every downstream table inherits: change the grain and every ratio in the report changes meaning.

blocks.label: daily revenue & buyers by country
blocks.code:
SELECT order_date::date AS day,
       country,
       SUM(amount)            AS revenue,
       COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) AS buyers
FROM orders
GROUP BY order_date::date, country;
blocks.pg: -- PostgreSQL: GROUP BY fixes the (day, country) grain

items.q: The query above reports revenue per (day, country). What is the grain?
items.explain: GROUP BY day, country makes the grain (day, country): one output row (plus aggregates) per valid pair.

items.q: Why does the same query use COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) for buyers?
options: A buyer can place several orders in one day, so rows would double-count them
The grain forces one buyer per row
items.explain: Each order is a row; COUNT(*) would count orders, not buyers. COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) counts each user once per (day, country) group.

blocks.label: conditional aggregates
blocks.code:
-- Baseline: one row per status
SELECT status,
       COUNT(*)  AS n,
       SUM(amount) AS total
FROM orders
GROUP BY status;

-- FILTER: several conditional aggregates in a single scan, no GROUP BY needed
SELECT COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'paid')   AS paid_orders,
       SUM(amount) FILTER (WHERE status = 'paid') AS paid_gmv,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'pending') AS pending_orders
FROM orders;

-- CASE equivalent: identical numbers, different spelling
SELECT COUNT(CASE WHEN status = 'paid' THEN 1 END)    AS paid_orders,
       SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'paid' THEN amount END) AS paid_gmv,
       COUNT(CASE WHEN status = 'pending' THEN 1 END) AS pending_orders
FROM orders;
blocks.pg: -- FILTER clause is PostgreSQL standard; CASE form works everywhere
blocks.mysql: -- MySQL 8.0: no FILTER — use the SUM(CASE WHEN ... THEN ... END) spelling

blocks.md: MySQL 8.0 has no FILTER clause — reach for the CASE form (`SUM(CASE WHEN status='paid' THEN amount END)`) there. Both compute identical numbers; FILTER is the modern spelling and keeps the predicate next to the aggregate it decorates.

options: It removes rows from the result set
It applies only to the aggregate it decorates
It is a PostgreSQL-only join hint
items.explain: FILTER scopes a single aggregate to matching rows without altering the result set's other columns.

items.q: In SUM(CASE WHEN status='paid' THEN amount END), what does an unpaid order contribute?
items.explain: CASE returns NULL when no branch matches; SUM ignores NULLs, so unpaid orders add nothing while the row's other aggregates stay intact.

blocks.label: case pivot
blocks.code:
SELECT region,
       SUM(CASE WHEN date_trunc('month', order_date) = DATE '2024-01-01' THEN amount END) AS m1,
       SUM(CASE WHEN date_trunc('month', order_date) = DATE '2024-02-01' THEN amount END) AS m2
FROM orders
GROUP BY region;
blocks.pg: -- PostgreSQL: date_trunc('month', ...) buckets to the 1st of the month
blocks.mysql: -- MySQL 8.0: use DATE_FORMAT(order_date, '%Y-%m-01') instead of date_trunc

blocks.label: crosstab() version
blocks.code:
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS tablefunc;

-- Two-argument crosstab: (row query, category query)
-- The category query's values become column names; you DECLARE their types below.
SELECT *
FROM crosstab('SELECT region, date_trunc(''month'', order_date)::date AS m, SUM(amount)
              FROM orders GROUP BY 1, 2 ORDER BY 1, 2',
              'SELECT DISTINCT date_trunc(''month'', order_date)::date AS m FROM orders ORDER BY 1')
     AS ct (region text, m1 numeric, m2 numeric);
blocks.pg: -- crosstab() from the tablefunc extension; output columns must be declared manually
blocks.mysql: -- MySQL 8.0: no crosstab() — use the CASE pivot or a prepared statement

blocks.md: Two-argument `crosstab(row_sql, category_sql)` pairs every row of the first query with a category list produced by the second. The output shape (`AS ct (…)`) is written by you — crosstab can't infer column names or types from the SQL strings. That manual declaration is exactly what makes dynamic pivots tricky (see L4).

items.q: Why must crosstab() output column types be declared explicitly?
options: Because column names must be quoted
Because the second query's values become column names with unknown types
Because crosstab is not a function
items.explain: The category values become output columns; PostgreSQL needs the explicit AS ct (...) column list with types.

items.q: The CASE pivot needs which clause to collapse many order rows into one row per region?
items.explain: GROUP BY region condenses the raw rows; each SUM(CASE ...) fills one month column of that region's pivot row.

revisionCard: Grain = the unit of observation a result row is unique by (e.g. one row per (day, country)); pick it before writing SQL
COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(column) skips NULLs; COUNT(DISTINCT column) counts unique non-null values
FILTER (WHERE …) scopes one aggregate; CASE scopes one value — identical math, FILTER is the modern spelling
CASE pivot: one SUM(CASE …) per column inside GROUP BY; crosstab() rotates without hand-written expressions
crosstab() output columns must be declared in AS ct (…); the category query decides which columns exist

glossary.def: The unit of observation a result set is unique by — e.g. one row per (day, country).
A quantifiable number computed from rows (revenue, buyers, GMV).
A label used to slice or group rows (day, country, region).
A pivot report rotating row-dimension values into columns; done with CASE aggregation or crosstab().
AGG(expr) FILTER (WHERE cond) — a conditional aggregate that scopes only the aggregate it decorates.
A metric that sums correctly across grains (revenue); non-additive metrics (distinct buyers) need explicit re-aggregation per grain.
